name: Threading kit
lead: Threading is a hair-removal method, used mainly on eyebrows and facial hair, in which a doubled and twisted cotton or polyester thread is rolled over unwanted hair so that it is pulled out at the follicle [1][2]. A threading kit is the consumer version of the tool: thread (sometimes with a handle or tensioning aid) that allows the technique to be tried at home rather than at a salon.

The technique is described as an ancient practice that originated in the Middle East and South Asia and later spread to Western countries [1][2]. It is typically performed in three ways, with the thread held by hand, by mouth or around the neck, and the mouth method is described as the fastest and most precise [2].

Published research is thin. A 2009 review in Clinical and Experimental Dermatology discussed the procedure's popularity and its "seldom-discussed complications" [1], and no controlled trials comparing threading with waxing or tweezing appear in the available literature. Results are temporary, as with other forms of epilation.
infobox: Middle East and South Asia, centuries old [2]
No device clearance applicable to plain thread

paras: A thin thread is doubled, twisted and rolled along the skin so that rows of short hairs are caught and lifted out at once, unlike tweezing which removes hairs one at a time [2]. It is used chiefly for eyebrows, but also the upper lip and other facial areas; sources describe it as unsuited to arms and legs, where hair is coarser and more extensive [2].

Threading is described as centuries old and as having begun in the Middle East and South Asia, where it was in some places linked to rites of passage such as preparation for marriage [2]. In Taiwan, women have traditionally had facial threading before the Lunar New Year [2]. Threading salons are reported to have spread in Germany in the 1980s and to have opened in large US cities from the late 1980s, run by immigrants from the Middle East and South Asia [2].

Sources cited by Wikipedia credit threading with finer control of eyebrow shape and with being gentler on skin than waxing, though these are descriptive claims rather than trial findings [2]. As an epilation method it is temporary, with hair growing back over time.
Threading can be painful because several hairs are pulled at once [2]. A dermatology review noted that, despite its popularity, the procedure has complications that are seldom discussed [1].
No studies found for home threading kits. The only peer-reviewed item identified is a narrative review of the salon procedure and its complications [1].

refs.title: Eyebrow threading: a popular hair-removal procedure and its seldom-discussed complications

card.summary: Twisted-thread plucking for brows and face: precise and cheap, temporary, barely studied.
card.note: Technique has little formal research; complications are rarely discussed.

quick.overview:
Threading uses a twisted thread to pull rows of fine hairs out at the follicle, mostly to shape eyebrows and clean up facial hair. A kit lets people try the technique at home.

It is an old technique with a long salon tradition. Hair grows back, so results are temporary, and published research is limited to a review of its complications.
quick.mechanism: A doubled, twisted thread is rolled across the skin, trapping hairs and lifting them out at the root in quick succession.
quick.risks: Pain, skin irritation and other complications have been described in a dermatology review. No formal trials compare it with waxing or tweezing.
